title: North Korea’s ‘Victory Day’ takes place with Kim Jong Un’s power transformed
gist: North Korea's Korean War 'Victory Day' mythology remains a fabrication, but Pyongyang's actual strategic position has inverted since 2019: Russia now depends on Kim Jong Un for artillery, ballistic missiles and combat troops for Ukraine, and Xi Jinping has publicly proposed expanded China-DPRK military exchanges. Kim has converted expendable manpower and munitions into sanctions erosion, Russian material support and simultaneous courtship by both Moscow and Beijing.

insights.claim: The Russia-North Korea relationship has flipped since Putin and Kim Jong Un first met in Vladivostok in April 2019: Russia now depends on Pyongyang for artillery shells, ballistic missiles and combat troops for the Ukraine war, rather than Kim seeking Russian patronage.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Sanctions-based containment of DPRK is structurally broken while Russia needs its output; price the Korean peninsula as a live escalation vector rather than a frozen one.
insights.quote: Russia now depends on Kim for artillery shells, ballistic missiles and, most importantly, combat troops to support its war in Ukraine.
insights.locator: Seven years later, the power dynamic

insights.claim: The 2019 Vladivostok summit showed Kim Jong Un's then-marginal status: Putin spent only a few hours with him before flying to Beijing, leaving Kim to attend a memorial ceremony alone, arriving over two hours late and staying seven minutes.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The 2019 baseline is the benchmark for measuring how fast a sanctioned state can re-rate its geopolitical leverage when a great power's war creates demand for its exports.
insights.locator: Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting Kim

insights.claim: Volodymyr Zelenskyy alleged on 25 July that Russia is preparing to receive as many as 30,000 additional North Korean soldiers and that Pyongyang is readying more ballistic-missile launchers for Moscow — unconfirmed by either government but plausible given the changed relationship.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A step from ~14,000 to ~30,000 additional troops would materially extend Russia's manpower runway in Ukraine and push out ceasefire timelines markets have partly discounted.
insights.locator: Indeed, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alleged on 25 July

themes.theme: Victory Day mythology as regime infrastructure

insights.claim: North Korea's 'Victory Day' rests on two documented falsehoods — that the US and South Korea started the Korean War, and that North Korea won it — when in fact Kim Il Sung invaded across the 38th parallel on 25 June 1950 and the 27 July 1953 armistice produced no decisive victor.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Regime legitimacy is built on a rewritten defeat, which means Pyongyang can convert any future costly engagement into domestic 'victory' — lowering its threshold for accepting losses.
insights.quote: North Korea’s ‘Victory Day’ has always rested on two foundational falsehoods .
insights.locator: ‘Victory Day’ – marking a war that wasn’t won

insights.claim: Pyongyang is manufacturing a second founding myth by honouring soldiers killed in Russia, providing new housing for their families and opening a memorial complex to their battlefield exploits, fashioning the post-2024 deployments into a new victorious generation.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Domestic mythologization of the Russia deployment signals it is a durable policy pillar, not an opportunistic one-off — expect continued troop and munitions flows.
insights.quote: The troops sent to Russia since 2024 are being fashioned into a new victorious generation.
insights.locator: Pyongyang is now incorporating the Ukrainian deployment

insights.claim: Western observers who read Victory Day ceremonies as evidence of pariah status — an isolated Stalinist state on Chinese life support with no agency beyond its nuclear programme — are working from an outdated model of North Korean power.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Consensus underweights DPRK as an independent actor; the mispricing is in treating Korean peninsula risk as static background noise.
insights.quote: The story of the war remains false, but the state celebrating it is more formidable than ever before.
insights.locator: To Western observers, the Victory Day ceremonies

themes.theme: From Hanoi humiliation to doctrinal hardening

insights.claim: Kim Jong Un's 2019 low point was the Hanoi summit, where he travelled 4,000 km by train to offer dismantling part of the Yongbyon nuclear complex for sanctions relief and Donald Trump rejected the offer and abruptly left.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The failed transactional template explains why Pyongyang now refuses denuclearization talks; any renewed US outreach starts from a far weaker bargaining position.
insights.locator: In February that year, Kim Jong Un travelled 4,000 km

insights.claim: Rather than retreat after 2019, North Korea enshrined nuclear status in its constitution, broadened the conditions for nuclear use, repeatedly rejected denuclearization as a negotiating object, and reclassified South Korea as its principal enemy with reunification declared impossible.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Denuclearization-for-sanctions-relief is off the table as a policy scenario; models assuming an eventual deal-driven de-risking of the peninsula are stale.

insights.claim: Since 2019 North Korea has significantly advanced solid-fuel ICBM technology, tactical nuclear systems, submarine-related capabilities, military reconnaissance satellites and drones — enough to credibly threaten South Korea and Japan and increasingly the continental United States, despite Pyongyang's habit of exaggerating technical feats.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rising credible threat to Japan and South Korea supports a structural bid for regional defence spending and missile-defence procurement.
insights.quote: North Korea can now threaten South Korea and Japan with an expanding range of nuclear and conventional systems while presenting an increasingly credible nuclear threat to the continental United States.
insights.locator: Of course, North Korea does exaggerate its technical feats.

themes.theme: Ukraine war as North Korea's payoff mechanism

insights.claim: Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine created the opening: as Russian losses mounted and reserves dwindled, North Korea supplied enormous quantities of artillery ammunition and ballistic missiles and dispatched approximately 14,000 troops to the Kursk region following a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty in June 2024.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: DPRK munitions capacity is a real variable in Russian artillery tempo; watch it as a proxy for how long Moscow can sustain attritional fighting.
insights.locator: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 gave Kim an opportunity.

insights.claim: Russia's payback to Pyongyang has been structural, not just financial: it shielded North Korea diplomatically, dismantled UN monitoring of sanctions violations, and reportedly supplied money, fuel, food and military assistance.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The destruction of the UN sanctions monitoring architecture is effectively irreversible in the near term — assume enforcement decay across other sanctioned regimes too.
insights.locator: Russia has shielded North Korea diplomatically

insights.claim: The deployment gave North Korean troops real combat experience in drone-dominated warfare, infantry operations under fire and adaptation on a modern battlefield — a qualitative upgrade to a force that had not fought a war since 1953.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A combat-blooded, drone-literate DPRK army raises the assessed conventional threat on the peninsula independent of the nuclear file.
insights.quote: Its troops have gained experience in drone-dominated warfare, infantry operations under fire and adaptation on a modern battlefield.
insights.locator: As a result, North Korea has seen military, economic and political gains.

insights.claim: The most consequential outcome is demonstrative rather than material: Kim has proved that an impoverished state can hold resources a major power urgently needs and cannot readily obtain on comparable terms.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A replicable template — scarce, ethically-unconstrained supply beats economic size as a source of leverage; applies to other sanctioned suppliers of munitions and manpower.
insights.quote: Most consequentially, Kim has demonstrated that his impoverished country possesses resources that a major power urgently needs and cannot readily obtain on comparable terms.

themes.theme: Beijing's reassessment and Sino-Russian competition for Pyongyang

insights.claim: Xi Jinping travelled to Pyongyang in June 2026 and, in a column in the party newspaper Rodong Sinmun, repeatedly called for 'strategic' cooperation and greater exchanges between the Chinese and North Korean militaries — described as an unprecedented public proposal by a Chinese leader.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: An explicit Chinese military-exchange offer is a discrete escalation signal in US-China strategic competition; watch for follow-through in joint exercises or exchanges.
insights.quote: called for greater exchanges between the Chinese and North Korean militaries – an unprecedented public proposal by a Chinese leader
insights.locator: President Xi Jinping travelled to Pyongyang in June

insights.claim: Beijing's posture has shifted from managing a troublesome neighbour to cultivating a prime asset in its strategic competition with the United States, even though it still prizes stability, remains wary of Pyongyang's provocations, and has not formed the battlefield alliance Russia has.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: China is no longer a reliable brake on DPRK behaviour — remove 'Beijing restrains Pyongyang' from base-case peninsula risk models.
insights.quote: not merely as a troublesome neighbour to be managed, but as a prime asset to be cultivated amid its strategic competition with the United States

insights.claim: Xi's June 2019 first visit to Pyongyang, reciprocating Kim's four trips to China, delivered pageantry but neither substantial economic relief nor strategic elevation — reaffirming Kim as the junior partner, in direct contrast to the 2026 visit.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The 2019-versus-2026 comparison is the cleanest evidence that Chinese valuation of North Korea has genuinely repriced, not merely rhetorically softened.
insights.locator: Then, in June 2019, President Xi finally reciprocated

insights.claim: North Korea's leverage comes not from scale — its economy is diminutive and its population impoverished — but from a portfolio of scarce assets: nuclear weapons, missiles, ammunition, expendable manpower, geostrategic location and an unusual willingness to accept risk, which now makes both Moscow and Beijing compete for influence over it.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Competition between two patrons gives Pyongyang bargaining power neither can unilaterally curb, meaning any Western sanctions or deterrence strategy premised on great-power cooperation is obsolete.
insights.quote: Yet it possesses scarce and valuable assets: nuclear weapons, missiles, ammunition, expendable manpower, a geostrategic location and an unusual willingness to accept risks.
insights.locator: Of course, North Korea is no equal of China or Russia

insights.claim: Treating Victory Day as an absurd pageant is itself the analytical error: the mythology is still false in 2026, but the power standing behind it has become ominously real.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reprice DPRK from a comic-opera tail risk to a structural feature of the Russia-China-US strategic triangle.
insights.quote: In 2026, that false mythology endures – but the power standing behind it has become ominously real.
insights.locator: On 27 July, Kim once again celebrates a war
